hook: Hear a radio gloss praise a city's 'digital' portal and catch how every compliment quietly takes it apart.
intro: A radio gloss (Glosse), about 500 words, heard once: a presenter praises his city's new citizens' portal „Stadt direkt“ and takes the praise apart sentence by sentence. It opens with solemn mock praise – „Unsere Stadt ist digital.“ – and undercuts it at once with the poster that „man wegen der Baustelle davor leider nur mit dem Fernglas lesen kann“. It then works through a chain of contradictions (an activation code „Per Post“, an ID application you fill in online and then print out, complaints that are „ausgedruckt und in der Poststelle abgeheftet“, an invitation to a digitisation award that „kam per Fax“), quotes official jargon („medienbruchfrei“, „vollumfänglich, nachhaltig und bürgernah“) against everyday images, and ends with a punchline that catches the speaker himself. The eight questions ask what the target is, what individual sentences really mean, and which satirical technique is at work – none of them can be answered from the literal words alone.
tips[0].title: Mock praise: take the praise literally, then look at the facts
tips[0].text: The speaker never says "this is bad". He praises – and puts the evidence right next to the praise. When a sentence sounds like a press release, check the sentence after it: it usually contradicts it. The target is what the praise covers up, not the thing the speaker seems to attack.
tips[0].trap: „Ich will nicht ungerecht sein“ announces a concession but delivers the next attack – a concession in satire is usually a set-up.
tips[0].check.why: The praise is mock praise: the very next sentence supplies the fact that cancels it.
tips[0].visual.rows[0].a: Das Portal ist rund um die Uhr erreichbar.
tips[1].title: The contradiction is the joke
tips[1].text: Collect the pairs that cancel each other out: digital promise vs. paper reality. The shorter the second half, the harder the hit – note the one- and two-word sentences that follow a long, official-sounding one.
tips[1].check.why: The short second half contradicts the digital promise: an online form you have to print out.
tips[2].title: Register shifts: quoted jargon meets everyday images
tips[2].text: Official words are quoted – often explicitly („ich zitiere die Pressemitteilung“) – and then confronted with a drastic, concrete image or taken literally. The speaker is displaying the jargon, not adopting it. Ask: whose language is this, and what does the next phrase do to it?
tips[2].check.why: so steht es in der Broschüre marks it as quoted jargon, and the one-hour opening time that follows takes it apart.
tips[3].title: The punchline turns the satire on the speaker
tips[3].text: The last paragraph links every earlier contradiction into one loop and lets it catch the narrator: he is „digital angekommen“ and yet waits for a letter he must collect in person, by appointment. The final short sentence is the thesis.
tips[3].check.why: The narrator ends up doing exactly what he mocked, so the last short sentence turns the satire on him.
remember[0]: Mock praise → check the next sentence: it usually contradicts the praise.
remember[1]: Target = what the praise covers up (surface digitisation and self-congratulation), not digitisation as such.
remember[2]: Short follow-up sentences („Per Post.“, „Die Einladung kam per Fax.“) carry the contradiction.
remember[3]: Quoted jargon + drastic everyday image = register shift that exposes the jargon.
remember[4]: The punchline gathers the earlier contradictions into one loop.
exam: Satire and cabaret are a C2 exam listening text — and the only way to get the joke on German late-night television.
tips[0].check.q: 'Die neue Bibliothek ist ein Meisterwerk der Planung. Leider hat man die Bücherregale vergessen.' What is the speaker really saying?
tips[2].check.q: 'Unser Amt ist jetzt kundenorientiert, so steht es in der Broschüre. Geöffnet ist es dienstags von neun bis zehn.' Whose word is kundenorientiert?
tips[2].check.options[0]: The office's, which the speaker shows up
tips[2].check.answer: The office's, which the speaker shows up
tips[3].check.q: A satire about the 'paperless office' ends: 'Ich drucke diesen Text jetzt aus. Zur Sicherheit.' Who is caught by the punchline?
